items.stem: In right triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $C$. The leg opposite angle $A$ has length $3$ and the leg adjacent to angle $A$ has length $4$. Find $\sin A$.
items.hint: Sine compares the opposite side with the hypotenuse, so find the hypotenuse before you write the ratio.

items.stem: In a right triangle, the side opposite the acute angle $\theta$ has length $4$ and the hypotenuse has length $8$. Find the exact value of $\theta$, measured in radians.
items.hint: Build the ratio that pairs the opposite side with the hypotenuse, then ask which special angle has that value.
worked: The acute angle whose sine is $\dfrac{1}{2}$ measures $30^{\circ}$.

items.stem: A right triangle has legs of length $9$ and $12$, and $\theta$ is the acute angle adjacent to the leg of length $12$. A student writes the hypotenuse as $\sqrt{9^{2}+12^{2}}=9+12=21$ and reports $\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{21}=\dfrac{4}{7}$. What is the correct value of $\cos\theta$?
items.hint: A square root does not split across a plus sign; finish the addition underneath the radical before taking the root.
worked: $\theta$ sits next to the leg of length $12$, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{12}{15}$.

items.stem: In right triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $C$, and $\tan A=\dfrac{7}{24}$. Exactly one of the four statements below is true. Which one?
items.hint: Angles $A$ and $B$ add to $90^{\circ}$, so the leg opposite $A$ is the leg adjacent to $B$.
worked: $\tan A=\dfrac{7}{24}$ means the leg opposite $A$ is $7$ and the leg adjacent to $A$ is $24$, so the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{7^{2}+24^{2}}=\sqrt{625}=25$.
Viewed from $B$ the legs trade roles: the leg adjacent to $B$ is the $7$ and the leg opposite $B$ is the $24$.
So $\cos B=\dfrac{7}{25}$, while $\sin B=\dfrac{24}{25}$ and $\sin A=\dfrac{7}{25}$.

items.stem: In a right triangle the acute angle $\theta$ has an adjacent leg of length $x$ and an opposite leg of length $x\sqrt{3}$, where $x>0$. Simplify $\sin\theta$ completely.
items.hint: Combine $x^{2}$ and $\left(x\sqrt{3}\right)^{2}$ under one radical before you take the square root.
